stories.summary: An Evanston developer turned a roof replacement into an opportunity, installing 540 kilowatts of bifacial solar panels atop the Church Street Plaza complex. The panels will power the building's base systems and add clean energy right in the heart of downtown.
stories.extended_summary: When an inspection found the roof at Evanston's Church Street Plaza was nearing the end of its lifespan, developer Evan Meador saw something else up there: unused space. Instead of a simple replacement, Continuum Development installed a reflective solar-ready roof and topped it with bifacial panels that generate electricity from both direct sunlight and reflected light. When switched on in the coming weeks, the array will add 540 kilowatts of clean energy to a rooftop in the middle of downtown — enough to power the building's base systems, with a junction box ready to share power with a future building next door.

stories.title: ‘We Deserve It’: In Birmingham, Black Farmers Open Fountain Heights’ First Grocery Store in 70 years
stories.summary: Birmingham's Fountain Heights neighborhood just got its first grocery store in nearly 70 years. A Black-owned farming cooperative opened We All Eat Market, stocked with fresh produce from their own plots — and the whole community showed up to celebrate.
stories.extended_summary: For nearly 70 years, residents of Birmingham's Fountain Heights had no grocery store of their own. That changed on Nov. 7, when the Fountain Heights Farms Cooperative — a Black-owned urban farm founded in 2016 — threw open the doors of We All Eat Market. Shelves lined with bulk grains, fresh juice, and herbs grown by co-founder Christopher Gooden sit beside a produce stand stocked from the collective's own plots and farms across Alabama. The grand opening felt like a block party: hugs, cooking demos, and neighbors finally shopping close to home. "We deserve it," the community said — and now they've built it.

stories.title: Albany Park Taps Volunteers To Help Run Its Rat Birth Control Program
stories.summary: Albany Park is the latest Chicago neighborhood to try rat birth control — plant-based sausage bait that reduces fertility in rats over time. Volunteers are now trained to maintain 40 bait boxes, offering a non-toxic alternative to poison.
stories.extended_summary: There's something about the phrase 'rat birth control' that catches people's attention — just ask the Albany Park volunteers who showed up on a rainy afternoon to learn how to maintain 40 bait boxes scattered along Kimball and Lawrence avenues. The boxes hold plant-based sausages made with cottonseed oil that reduce fertility in male and female rats over time. It's a non-toxic alternative to poison, and Albany Park is the third Chicago neighborhood to partner with Arizona-based SenesTech after Lincoln Park and Wicker Park-Bucktown. For residents tired of rats scurrying past their garages, it's a surprisingly hopeful — and slightly funny — experiment.

stories.title: As Fish and Game studies pikas in a warming world, volunteers fill a gap
stories.summary: Volunteers are trekking up to 10 miles into Wyoming's backcountry to sit in silence and listen for squeaks — tracking American pikas, the tiny alpine mammals that can't survive extreme heat, as state wildlife officials study a warming world.
stories.extended_summary: Rachael Dunlop, a neuroscientist and wildlife photographer, dropped to her hands and rear to scramble across a loose rock field near the summit of Teton Pass, hot-pink rope in hand. It took her an hour to find the monitoring site — and that's moving fast. She's one of a few dozen volunteers who hike up to 10 miles one way into the backcountry to sit in silence, listening for squeaks and scanning shadows for droppings left by the American pika. This summer was one of Wyoming's warmest on record, and heat is a grave threat to the small mammals that live exclusively in the alpine. The volunteers are filling a gap for state wildlife officials studying how pikas fare in a warming world.

stories.title: Behind origins of BetterCampus
stories.summary: When schools locked down and a blank white Canvas screen got him down, George Mills built a browser extension to make assignments visible. That side project became BetterCampus — now a full ed-tech platform with 2.5 million users, shaped entirely by student feedback.
stories.extended_summary: "He got really depressed when that happened, because, I don't know, looking at a blank white screen all day kind of sucks," says Jake Silver of his co-founder George Mills, who was sent home when schools went into lockdown. Struggling to track assignments, Mills used his coding skills to build a browser extension that let students customize Canvas and see upcoming work in a to-do list. He shared it with friends and posted on Reddit — and the user base started growing. That idea became BetterCampus, now a full platform with tools like completed tasks, flashcards and note-taking, and 2.5 million users. Its development is still guided by the students who use it.

stories.title: Belmont Scout Earns Eagle Through Veterans Project
stories.summary: 14-year-old Max Ruban is earning his Eagle Scout rank by doing something totally different: recording local veterans' stories for the Library of Congress Veterans History Project. His scoutmaster calls the project 'fabulous' and 'so original.'
stories.extended_summary: Most Eagle Scout projects involve hammers and nails. Max Ruban, 14, went a different route: he's capturing the life stories of local veterans for the Library of Congress's Veterans History Project. The Belmont teen pitched the idea to his scoutmaster, a troop committee, and the regional Scouting council, then partnered with Waverly VFW Post 1272 as his beneficiary. His scoutmaster, Ben Amidon, was immediately sold. 'This is fabulous because it is so original,' he said. The project turns a rite of passage into a genuine act of preservation — giving veterans a permanent record and giving Max a rank he'll carry for life.

stories.title: Beyond the business plan: how Michigan Women Forward is helping Flint entrepreneurs turn ideas into opportunity
stories.summary: Michigan Women Forward is backing Flint entrepreneurs with loans, coaching, and a weekly Funding Desk. Tanesia Greer, who opened her first salon at 18, is one of the founders turning hard-won experience into new opportunity.
stories.extended_summary: Tanesia Greer was a shampoo assistant at 14, a salon owner at 18, and by her own account 'born to be my own boss.' Now she's one of the Flint entrepreneurs getting real backing from Michigan Women Forward, which is bringing loans, coaching, and a weekly Funding Desk to the city. Greer's story — no college degree, just a high school diploma and relentless work ethic — is exactly the kind of grit the program is designed to fuel. It's not just capital; it's mentorship and infrastructure for people who've already proven they can build something from nothing.

stories.title: Bogus Basin Saves 60% of Snow Through Idaho Summer
stories.summary: Bogus Basin stashed a giant pile of snow under insulated panels in March and came back in November to find about 60% of it still there — even after Idaho summer heat hit 118 degrees on the panel surfaces. The Finnish tech is called Snow Secure, and it basically let a mountain keep its winter through seven months of sun.
stories.extended_summary: Surface temperatures on those insulated panels reportedly hit a scorching 118 degrees this summer. Underneath, a giant pile of snow just waited it out — and roughly 60% of it survived. Bogus Basin's Mountain Operations team buried the snow back in late March using Snow Secure, a Finnish-developed insulation technology, then uncovered it in November to find most of their winter still intact. It's the kind of result that sounds like a cartoon, but it could mean real savings for ski seasons and snow storage in warming climates.

stories.title: Chester board hears of Mesh Network, new grants, Yosemite request
stories.summary: A Chester resident and his brother have been quietly building a low-frequency radio "mesh" network that lets neighbors text each other without cell service or electricity. It's designed to keep people connected when disasters knock out normal communications.
stories.extended_summary: For months, Chester resident Josh Johnson and his brother have been secretly building a network of low-frequency radio repeaters — and one of them was mistaken for a surveillance camera. The Chester Mesh Network lets residents send encrypted texts through small "companion" devices linked to their phones via Bluetooth, no cell service or electricity required. Messages hop from repeater to repeater, making it a lifeline when ice storms or floods take down normal communications. Johnson presented the system to the town board this week, explaining how individuals and groups get their own addresses and private messages stay encrypted end to end.

stories.title: Chimp Gets Food Delivered by Drone After Floodwaters Leave Him Stranded
stories.summary: When floodwaters stranded 38-year-old chimp Kaleb on a small island at a Florida sanctuary, caregivers didn't miss a beat — they flew his bananas and oranges in by drone. Video shows him happily pulling a banana from a paper bag dropped from above.
stories.extended_summary: Kaleb the chimpanzee was stranded on a tiny island surrounded by floodwater — so his caregivers sent in a drone. Heavy rains had submerged the roads at Save the Chimps sanctuary near Fort Pierce, cutting off food deliveries to the 38-year-old chimp. Staff loaded bananas, oranges, and blankets onto a delivery drone and flew them straight to him, and the sanctuary caught video of Kaleb happily pulling a banana from a paper bag dropped from the sky. "Chimps are getting all their food on time," facilities director Mark Yohannan said. "They haven't missed a beat." CEO Ana Paula Tavares swore she saw "a grateful look on his face."

stories.title: Colfax group gets $2.8M grant to switch Aurora luxury home project into affordable housing
stories.summary: After years of protesting luxury townhomes starting at $600K, the East Colfax Community Collective got a $2.8M state grant to buy the Aurora land itself. The plan: 152 units of affordable housing and community space instead of displacement.
stories.extended_summary: For years, the East Colfax Community Collective protested plans for luxury townhomes starting at $600,000 on a 1.34-acre lot in northwest Aurora. Now the community group owns the future of that land instead. A $2.8 million grant from a state affordable housing fund lets EC3 acquire the Ambience site and build 152 units of affordable housing plus community space. Organizer Jamie Laurie of Project Worthmore called it "a full circle moment." The collective has also purchased a 14-unit building nearby to preserve as naturally occurring affordable housing — bringing a whole block of Yosemite Street under community control and preventing displacement.

stories.title: Demystifying plug-in solar devices, which are now legal and can save Oaklanders money
stories.summary: Plug-in solar is now legal in California, and East Oakland's Ansel Troy is demystifying it one Instagram video at a time. His DIY backyard tutorials show residents how to cut utility costs with simple, safe, affordable setups — no 'solar magicians' required.
stories.extended_summary: "It's the most basic technology out there." That's Ansel Troy's message to anyone who thinks solar is only for the pros. The East Oakland tinkerer has been documenting his backyard experiments on Instagram (@tinyoakland), showing viewers where to buy plug-in units, whether a battery is worth it, and how to set everything up safely. His timing is perfect: in September, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a law allowing 1.2-kilowatt plug-in solar devices without utility permits or extra fees. Troy's growing audience is hungry for practical advice, and his videos make clean energy feel less like magic and more like something you could actually do this weekend.

stories.title: Dynamic teaching duo connects seniors and students through storytelling
stories.summary: Once Upon a Generation pairs students with local seniors, who get interviewed and then have their life stories performed by the kids. Founded in 2016 by two Massachusetts teachers, the 12-week program just got recognized by the state legislature for its 10th anniversary — and won a national storytelling award too.
stories.extended_summary: Karen Chace's son once asked who the beautiful 18-year-old in a photo was. It was his grandmother. That moment stuck with her — kids don't realize their grandparents had whole lives before them. So she teamed up with fellow East Freetown teacher Andrea Lovett, and in 2016 they launched Once Upon a Generation. Students from 4th through 12th grade interview a senior, then workshop and perform a story from that person's life. A decade later, the Massachusetts Legislature honored the program for its 10th anniversary, and the National Storytelling Network gave it the inaugural Angela Lloyd Sunbrella Award.

stories.title: El Pasoans Can Sponsor Headstones to Honor Forgotten Veterans
stories.summary: A project in El Paso lets community members sponsor replacement headstones for forgotten veterans buried at Concordia Cemetery — just $155 covers research, VA documentation, and installation. The initiative honors servicemen from the Civil War through World War I, including Buffalo Soldiers and a pioneering WWI aviator.
stories.extended_summary: At Concordia Cemetery in El Paso, some veterans' grave markers have crumbled, deteriorated, or vanished entirely. The Veterans Replacement Headstone Project is fixing that one stone at a time — and anyone can sponsor one for $155, which covers historical research, VA paperwork, and installation through a local monument company. The effort honors servicemen from the Civil War, Indian Wars (including Buffalo Soldiers), Spanish-American War, Mexican Revolution, and World War I. One recent restoration replaced the marker of 1st Lt. James "Buster" Biggs, a pioneering WWI Army aviator whose name now graces Biggs Army Airfield.

stories.title: Endangered, colorful garter snakes released into the wild for the first time
stories.summary: For the first time ever, 62 endangered San Francisco garter snakes born at the San Francisco Zoo were released into the wild in San Mateo County. The brilliantly colored reptiles have been on the endangered list since 1967, and only a few thousand remain — so this rewilding marks a real milestone for the species.
stories.extended_summary: The San Francisco garter snake is one of the most colorful reptiles in North America — and one of the rarest. It's been on the endangered species list since 1967, and after decades of drought, disease, invasive species, and poaching, only a few thousand remain. This fall, for the first time, 62 young snakes born at the San Francisco Zoo were released at sites across San Mateo County. Biologists call it a crucial step toward building self-sustaining populations, and it clears the way for more releases in the future.
